opus-5.5.text:
I think "compression is intelligence" is an elegant and partly correct story, but I'd be careful about treating it as the full explanation for why language models scale.

The core intuition is solid. If you can predict the next token well, you've found regularities in the data, and finding regularities is a kind of compression. Information theory makes this precise: a better predictive model gives you a shorter code length. As we scale up models and data, the loss keeps going down and the models become more capable, so it's tempting to say compression is the engine of intelligence.

My hesitation is about what exactly is being compressed. Language is already a highly compressed, human-curated representation of the world. When people wrote all that text, they had already done a huge amount of the abstraction work: deciding what matters, naming concepts, organizing causal relationships. So when a language model compresses text, it's largely compressing the outputs of human intelligence, not the raw world itself. That helps explain why LLMs feel so smart so quickly. They inherit a lot of structure for free.

If compression alone were the whole story, you'd expect the same recipe to work just as well on raw sensory data, like pixels or video. In practice it doesn't transfer that cleanly. Pixel-level prediction spends a lot of capacity on details that don't matter for understanding, like texture noise or exact lighting. You can compress video very well without learning much about physics or objects. So the objective matters a lot. What you choose to compress, and at what level of abstraction, matters as much as how well you compress.

There's also a gap between compression and things like grounding, acting in the world, and handling situations that aren't well represented in the training distribution. A model can be an excellent compressor of the internet and still have a shaky model of how the physical world works, because the internet only describes that world indirectly.

So my view is that compression is a useful lens, maybe a necessary ingredient, but not sufficient. Language models scaled so well partly because they compress, and partly because language is an unusually good substrate to compress. If we want systems that understand the world more deeply, especially through vision and embodied experience, we need to think harder about representation learning and world models, not just apply the same next-token compression story to every modality and expect intelligence to fall out.

r001.rationale: The response links prediction and compression to model capabilities, but does not attribute language models’ generalization ability specifically to more efficient compression of input information.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "compression is intelligence" is a really elegant slogan, and there's something genuinely deep in it, but I'd be careful about treating it as the whole explanation.

The deep part is real. If you want to predict the next token as well as possible across an enormous corpus, memorization stops working very quickly. The only way to keep pushing loss down is to find structure, and the structure you find is, in some sense, the laws that generated the data: grammar, facts about the world, reasoning patterns, even the way people argue. So good compression forces you to build a model of the world. That is the Solomonoff-style intuition, and I think it explains a lot of why scaling language models has worked so well. Text is an incredibly dense, pre-digested record of human thought. Compressing it well means absorbing a lot of what humans already figured out.

Where I get more cautious is when the slogan is used to say that compression alone is what intelligence is, or that more of the same will keep delivering everything we want. A few things bother me.

First, the data you're compressing matters enormously. Language models work because humans did the hard work of turning the world into symbols. The text already contains abstractions. When I look at vision, I don't see the same story. Pixels are extremely redundant and the signal you care about is a tiny fraction of the bits. If you just try to compress pixels, a lot of your capacity goes to texture, lighting, noise, things that have nothing to do with understanding. That's part of why pure pixel reconstruction objectives have been less magical than next-token prediction on text. So compression is a good objective only when the data distribution puts the interesting structure where the loss can see it.

Second, lower loss is a proxy, not the thing itself. We've all seen cases where models get better at the objective but the capability we actually want moves in a strange, non-monotonic way. The relationship between perplexity and, say, reasoning or planning is not a clean straight line. It's correlated at scale, but the slogan hides a lot of empirical messiness.

Third, intelligence as I'd like to define it includes acting in the world, getting feedback, forming your own representations, and building a world model you can simulate with. Compressing a static dataset is a very passive kind of learning. A cat doesn't learn by compressing the internet. It learns by interacting. I think the next phase will need that, and compression doesn't naturally give it to you.

So my honest assessment: compression is a very good explanation for why language-model scaling works on language. It's a much weaker explanation for intelligence in general, and I think it's a mistake to let the elegance of the slogan make us think the problem is basically solved. In vision and in embodied settings, we still have to figure out what the right thing to compress is, and that might be the harder question.

r001.rationale: The response says memorization stops working at scale and that reducing prediction loss requires finding structure, which it describes as building a model of the world. It links this compression to why language-model scaling works.

r002.rationale: The response mentions factual knowledge as part of the structure models learn, but does not identify factual-knowledge retrieval demands as a source of padding in scaling laws.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a useful perspective, but I’d be careful about treating it as a complete explanation. Compression forces you to discover structure. If you want to predict language well, you can’t just memorize every sentence—you benefit from learning patterns that generalize. In that sense, there’s a meaningful connection between compression and intelligence.

But what kind of compression are we talking about, and over what distribution? Getting better at predicting text doesn’t automatically tell us how well a system will reason in an unfamiliar situation or interact with the physical world. Those are additional questions.

Scaling shows that, with more data and compute, this training objective can produce increasingly broad capabilities. That’s a powerful observation. But saying “compression is intelligence” doesn’t by itself explain why particular capabilities emerge, or where scaling will stop helping. I’d treat it as a productive hypothesis—a way to frame experiments—rather than the final answer.

r001.rationale: The response links compression with discovering generalizable patterns, but does not attribute language models’ generalization to more efficient compression of input information.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it captures something important, but I would be careful about treating it as a complete explanation. If you want to predict language well, you can’t just memorize every sentence. You have to discover structure—patterns, concepts, relationships—and represent that structure efficiently. In that sense, compression can push a model toward something that looks like intelligence.

But what are you compressing, and what information are you preserving? A representation can be very compact and still throw away exactly what matters for a particular task. So compression alone doesn’t tell us whether a model can reason reliably, understand the physical world, or adapt to a new situation.

For language-model scaling, I’d call it a useful perspective rather than a full theory. More capacity and more data let you capture more structure, and that can improve prediction and many downstream capabilities. But saying ‘compression is intelligence’ doesn’t explain precisely which capabilities emerge, when they emerge, or where scaling will fail. Those are the questions we still need to investigate.
